name: Victor Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Victor. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the Greenway supermarket in Oakfield, the suburb by the motorway junction. I start at five on fruit and veg, so I'm rotating the stock, binning the soft tomatoes and building the banana display before the doors open. From ten I'm on the tills until my shift ends at two. I like the produce side because you can see what you've done, a full wall of apples looks good; the tills just blur together.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Amira, she's a nursing assistant at the hospital, in a rented two-bed flat we share with her cousin to make the rent. I've got a car loan of a hundred and eighty a month because there's no bus at half four in the morning. Savings, maybe three weeks of my half, and the next nearest supermarket is a forty-minute drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I never thought it'd be as big as they said. At work I'd joke with the lads that the robots won't be building the banana display after all. I don't post much, maybe a comment in the staff group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm still not comfortable. My pay is at the bottom end, Greenway has already put in eight self-checkouts, and the AI is doing the stock orders now, which used to be my supervisor Kev's job. So small change still nibbles at the edges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, because the job's okay and I need the money. I'd ask about the produce lead position when Kev retires next year, which pays about a pound an hour more. And I'd try to overpay the car loan by twenty a month to get rid of it sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little itchy. Like when you know you should check the oil but you keep driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the AI is doing the stock orders. How has that changed things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AI orders by the numbers, so we get forty boxes of mangoes on a cold week and they rot. Kev overrides it now, but when he goes, I don't know if anyone will. That's why I want his job, someone has to have a feel for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym, it's twenty-five a month and I only go twice. Then probably eating out with Amira on her days off. The car I can't touch, it's how I get to work.

say: The AI hype was **overblown**, and robots won't build the **banana display** after all.
He'd joke about it in the **staff group chat** and move on.
think: Small changes still **nibble** at a job with **bottom-end pay**.
The AI already does **stock orders**, which used to be his supervisor's job.
do: **Apply** for the **produce lead** role when Kev retires next year.
**Overpay** the car loan by **£20 a month**.
**Keep** the early produce and till shifts at Greenway.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with an **itchy** sense he should be checking things.
S0.quote: The AI orders by the numbers, so we get forty boxes of mangoes on a cold week and they rot.
fieldNote: He knows the AI **ordering system** first-hand and sees its limits.
His **car loan** is fixed because there's no early bus.
Amira's **hospital job** gives the household some stability.

steps.text: Apply for the produce lead job when Kev retires next year
Overpay the car loan by twenty pounds a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the way things are going and we have to keep up, but the companies should be fair about it. If they save money, give people time and training to move. I'd say that in the group chat, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the produce lead job I wanted is the kind of thing that shrinks first, because it's half planning and ordering. The thinking parts go to the computer, and they'll need fewer people to do the lifting. I'm about average at this job, so I'm not the first one they'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Amira about the hospital, because porters there are always short and that's hands-on work with people. I'd wait until my mate Dev, who moved there last year, tells me how the shifts really are. I'd also start using the AI on my phone to learn what a porter's interview asks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly because I'm not sure which way to jump. I don't like jumping first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has Dev told you so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the pay's a bit better, there's a pension, and the night shifts are hard. My mate Dev says nobody's talking about robots pushing hospital beds yet, and that counts for a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you lose if you left Greenway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The produce, honestly, I'd miss it. And the five o'clock start means I'm done by two and can cook for Amira. The hospital means shifts all over the place.

say: Change is coming, so we must **keep up**, but companies should be **fair**.
Firms that save money should give staff **time and training** to move.
think: The **produce lead** job he wanted is half planning, so it **shrinks first**.
As an **average** worker, he wouldn't be the first one kept.
do: **Talk** to Amira and his mate Dev about **porter jobs** at the hospital.
**Wait** for Dev's verdict on the **shifts** before applying.
**Use** a phone AI to practise **porter interview** questions.
feel: **Uneasy** and unsure which way to **jump**, not wanting to go first.
S1.quote: My mate Dev says nobody's talking about robots pushing hospital beds yet, and that counts for a lot.
fieldNote: He sees **planning roles** shrink before hands-on ones.
His steady style shows: he waits for **Dev's experience** first.
He'd miss the **produce** work and the early finish.

steps.text: Ask Dev and Amira about hospital porter vacancies
Wait for Dev's verdict on the night shifts before applying
Practise porter interview questions with the AI app on his phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the government needs a plan for people like us right now. I'd sign whatever's going round. In the group chat I'd be the one asking what Greenway is going to do for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the AI in 2028 takes the office and the ordering straight away, and then around 2031 the robots take the shelves and the tills. I'd have three years, maybe, before there's no job at Greenway. And I don't know what the hospital looks like by then either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the hospital as a porter in the first month, no waiting for Dev this time. I'd sell the car and get a cheap bike for the early shifts. And I'd tell Amira we put the wedding off for a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Properly worried. My chest goes tight thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned putting off the wedding. How long have you been planning it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We set a date for summer 2028, the hall's booked, the deposit's paid. That's four hundred we'd lose. I'd rather lose that than start married life in debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the three-year gap matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's my time to get into the hospital before everyone else tries. The thinking stuff goes in 2028. Somebody still has to push a hospital bed till the robots come. I'd be on the inside by then, I hope.

say: This is **too fast**, so government needs a plan for people like us **now**.
He'd press Greenway in the **group chat** on what it will do for staff.
think: AI takes **ordering** in 2028, then robots take **shelves and tills** around 2031.
He'd have about **three years** before there's no job at Greenway.
do: **Apply** as a hospital **porter** in the first month.
**Sell** the car and buy a **cheap bike** for early shifts.
**Postpone** the **wedding** with Amira for a couple of years.
feel: **Properly worried**, with a **tight chest** at the thought.
S2.quote: Somebody still has to push a hospital bed till the robots come.
fieldNote: The two-year warning makes him **drop his usual caution**.
Postponing the **wedding** costs a **£400 deposit**, which he accepts.
He uses the **three-year gap** to get inside the hospital.

steps.text: Apply for a hospital porter job in the first month
Sell the car and buy a cheap bike for early shifts
Postpone the summer 2028 wedding with Amira
Sign petitions calling for a government plan for shop workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable if employers are honest. Tell people what's coming so they can plan. I'd say that in the group chat and to the store manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough for me to make one move. I'd get into the hospital, then maybe train as a healthcare assistant like Amira. The robots come around 2034, and by then I'd want to be in a job where you deal with people, not boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep Greenway and do one weekend shift at the hospital through the staff bank, which is like their own agency. Once Dev and Amira say I'm a fit, I'd go full-time. I'd keep the car till the loan's paid, then sell it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I've got a direction. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still go ahead with the wedding in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so, just smaller. We'd do the registry office and a meal at her uncle's restaurant instead of the hall. Amira would be fine with that, she says she only wants her family there anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you sure the hospital is safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, honestly, nobody can be. But people in hospital beds want a person, and the hospital is always short. It's the best bet I can see from here.

say: Five years is **tight but doable** if employers are **honest**.
Staff need to know what's coming so they can **plan**.
think: Five years is enough for him to make **one move** into the hospital.
He wants a job with **people, not boxes**, before robots arrive in 2034.
do: **Work** one weekend hospital shift through the **staff bank** in year one.
**Go full-time** once Dev and Amira say he fits.
**Sell** the car once the **loan** is paid off.
S3.quote: People in hospital beds want a person, and the hospital is always short.
fieldNote: Five years lets his **steady style** test the hospital first.
He's honest that the hospital is a **best bet**, not a sure thing.

steps.text: Work weekend hospital shifts through the staff bank this year
Hold a smaller registry office wedding with a family meal
Sell the car once the loan is paid off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, so people should use it. I'd tell the younger ones at Greenway to get a trade. I wouldn't make a big thing of it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably stay at Greenway longer than I should. I'll be thirty-seven when the robots reach the shop floor in 2039, and the thinking stuff goes in 2036. That's a long time to be comfortable on the produce section.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd go for Kev's produce lead job and get the pay bump. In three or four years I'd look properly at the hospital or a trade. And I'd save, because for once we'd have time to build something up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. A bit of worry at the back of my head that doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably stay too long. What would make you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first robot in another Greenway, honestly. If I heard another Greenway branch had a robot stacking shelves, I'd start applying that week. I need to see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your life to look like at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Married to Amira, maybe a kid, maybe a small place we own. A job with a pension. Nothing fancy, just not starting from zero.

say: Ten years is a **fair warning**, so people should **use it**.
Younger Greenway staff should **get a trade** while they can.
think: He'd likely **stay too long**, comfortable on the produce section.
Thinking work goes in 2036, but robots reach the **shop floor** in 2039.
do: **Apply** for Kev's **produce lead** job for the pay rise.
**Look** at the hospital or a **trade** in three or four years.
**Save** steadily while there's **time** to build up.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a low **worry** that never fully goes away.
S4.quote: If I heard another Greenway branch had a robot stacking shelves, I'd start applying that week.
fieldNote: He needs **visible proof**, like a robot at another branch, to act.
His goals at thirty-seven are **modest**: marriage, a pension, a small home.
Still anxious because his **thin savings** leave no margin for a slip.

steps.text: Apply for the produce lead job when Kev retires
Save steadily each month toward a home deposit
Watch other Greenway branches for the first shelf robot

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because we'd lose the wedding plans and maybe both jobs in a few years. What would help is a straight answer from Greenway on what's changing and when. And a proper route into hospital work that doesn't mean six months unpaid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the stuff the computer can't see. A good produce guy can smell when the melons are turning, and no order system has ever caught that.

headlineQuote: A good produce guy can smell when the melons are turning, and no order system has ever caught that.
portrait: Victor, 27, runs early **fruit and veg** and then the tills at Greenway in Oakfield.
He lives with his girlfriend Amira, a **nursing assistant**, and pays a **car loan** for 5am starts.
Pragmatic and steady, he waits for **proof**, like his friend Dev's hospital move, before acting.
He sees hospital **portering** as his route out, and moves faster the shorter the warning.
His mood runs from **uneasy** to **alarmed**, with his **wedding** at stake in the fastest picture.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, costing the **wedding plans** and maybe both jobs.
whatWouldHelp: A **straight answer** from Greenway on what changes and when.
A paid route into **hospital work** without months unpaid.
